adds.title: LGBT rights in Turkey — Wikipedia
adds.summary: Turkey has permitted transgender people to change their legal gender since 1988, but only with sex-reassignment surgery, a medical examination and court permission; there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are not available. Because Turkish marriage law determines eligibility by the gender recorded in a person's civil registry rather than by trans status, an individual who has legally changed registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026, provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people were removed from the bill, though it made symbolic same-sex weddings possible that carry no legal marital status.

adds.title: World Report 2025: Türkiye — Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: HRW (World Report 2025, covering 2024) records that the Erdoğan government and religious conservative opposition parties regularly use discriminatory speech amounting to hate speech against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender communities on the pretext of promoting family values, putting LGBT people at great risk. Istanbul Pride was banned for the tenth consecutive year, and many cities across the country impose similar bans, which means a trans traveler's prospects of participating in visible LGBT assembly in Mersin-area cities face the same national ban pattern.

adds.title: World Report 2024: Türkiye — Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: HRW (World Report 2024, covering 2023) records that the Erdoğan government made anti-LGBT hate speech a core part of its election campaign, and that the ninth successive ban on Istanbul Pride week events in June was accompanied by police arrests of those who attempted to assemble. Authorities regularly and arbitrarily ban other events by LGBT groups, and local authorities around the country have increasingly canceled concerts by artists openly supportive of LGBT rights; TV regulator RTÜK has justified fines on digital platforms for LGBT-related content as violating 'societal and cultural values.' These nationwide enforcement patterns reach resort-province institutions like Muğla's, coloring what any visible LGBT assembly there can expect.
